subject: chemistry-1
question: A proton has a mass of about 1.00728 amu and an electron about 0.00054858 amu. Which statement best explains why an atom's mass is treated as residing almost entirely in its nucleus?

options.text: Electrons are massless particles, so only nucleons can contribute to the mass of an atom
Electrons are excluded from mass totals because they carry negative rather than positive charge
A proton is roughly 1,836 times as massive as an electron, so protons and neutrons supply nearly all of the mass
The nucleus occupies most of the atom's volume, so it necessarily holds most of the atom's mass

explanation:
Dividing the two masses gives 1.00728 / 0.00054858, or about 1,836, and a neutron is slightly heavier still than a proton. In a carbon-12 atom the six electrons together contribute roughly 0.03 percent of the total mass, which is why mass number counts only nucleons. Charge is unrelated to mass; electrons have small but real mass; and the nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller in radius than the atom, so it holds nearly all the mass in a tiny fraction of the volume.

ELI-10: It takes about 1,836 electrons stacked together to match the mass of one proton. Neutrons weigh about the same as protons, so every particle in the nucleus is a heavyweight and every electron outside it is a featherweight. Even in a large atom with dozens of electrons, all of them together still add up to a rounding error compared with the nucleus. That is why chemists count only protons and neutrons when they talk about an atom's mass, and why the tiny nucleus carries nearly all of the weight despite taking up almost none of the space.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
